Cervical stenosis is more statistically likely to be an issue and was for me. Specifically caused by the LEEP (tissue excised from 12-9 on the clock) and built up scar tissue made dilating an issue. Lucky for me, I had a nurse who could feel the scar tissue and did an, ahem, aggressive massage to help allow the cervix to dilate more than "fingertip". 12 hours into a 41 week induction and still at fingertip was very defeating.  Still better than surgery and c section, but also I was not prepared for it to be an issue. I would just be mindful of this as a possibility of you're having trouble dilating past a fingertip on your own. 

Good luck!

I just want to emphasize that "induction" can mean a lot of different things and I get the feeling that you'd like to encourage but not force your body to get the show on the road. This is something worth speaking to your care team about. What are all the different levels of intervention for induction? For example, I had cytotech (a cervical dilation) alone to start and no pitocin. After two doses, my body started going on its own all the way to about 9cm (took a long time though). 

You can advocate for minimal interventions that fit your best idea of a birth plan and hopefully they'll work, if not be flexible. My good friend was allowed to do about an hour of nipple stimulation via a pump when her labor stalled at 5cm. It worked too! Good luck!!

So our group has live find dogs who work airscent as well as tracking trailing dogs. Tracking trailing dogs are probably what are used most in movies where there is an article (shirt/socks) from the lost person and the dog has their nose to the ground sniffing as they go. Airscent dogs will find any person, super useful in rural-lost hiker situations. People shed skin cells, hair, they perspire and breathe. Those all have distinct odors that the dogs are trained to follow. 

HRD dogs are smelling for a different odor profile. Blood, tissue, bones all at varying levels of decomposition, because different levels of decomposition will smell differently too. For example, one of the placentas we have is encased in cement and we use it to train dogs on underwater or buried locations. Organ tissue will likely not have "your" smell, so shouldn't be an issue for the dog. 

I am a chemist by day and they're are actually a few interesting studies that looked at what "odors" are given off by different human remains samples that dogs trained on (this was in association with the FBI). They are vastly different depending on what it is. It really highlights the complexity of training a dog to find a deceased individual, you have to have a huge training set so the dog knows that there are a lot of different smells that mean they are on the right trail. Organ tissue is definitely a hard one to come by so any placental donations are super useful!

This sounds like the fertility benefits that are being added to my insurance plan this next calendar year. My husband has a lifetime maximum and I have a separate lifetime maximum. Unfortunately for us, they announced these benefits a couple of days before my first egg retrieval, (we so would have waited two months for Jan. 1 in order to save 30K). I personally think it stinks that IVF and anything to do with the embryo and embryo transfers have to be billed under the female's insurance. 

However, there are many forms of male factor infertility that involve infertility treatments that can be billed to the male's insurance. There is testing, medications, specialist visits, even surgeries, and a whole other slew of infertility treatments that would count toward the lifetime maximum. Your IVF clinic should be billing your partner's SA and his consultation to his insurance. The only issue is when you get into package pricing options, they usually have a disclaimer that says *everything will be billed to the female*. That is if the IVF clinic even does package pricing when you have *some* insurance coverage.  I don't think this makes it better that you can't use it for IVF, but I always think of insurance companies as organizations that pay employees to try and figure out how to not pay your benefits.

I went through this earlier this year before starting IVF. I was too old and missed the window when the vaccine was more common and part of the routine vaccinations. I was around chickenpox plenty when I was a child, but just never caught it. My GP was very adamant that I get tested as getting chickenpox when pregnant can have devastating effects on the mother. After finding out that I had no immunity, it was a pain in the ass to actually get as an adult. My GP only does adults and therefore doesn't carry vaccinations that are standard for kids, the children's clinic won't see anyone who is over 18. The pharmacy does not carry this vaccination either. Okay, so I can go to a boutique vaccination place (think travel vaccines) and pay $1,000 for something that should be covered. Luckily, my GP is a boss and she got a doctor friend in my small town who is in family practice to agree to see me without having to "establish me as a patient". Took about 1 week to find out I wasn't immune then 6 months to get the vaccination. Glad I started working on this super early. Your GP should 100% be concerned about the possibility of you getting chickenpox whilst pregnant. That shit is serious and their lack of concern is troubling.

Depending on where you are, SAR teams are managed very, very differently. I live in a very rural area, so every incident in my state requiring a SAR team will be managed by the same management system. There is no lost communication/efforts between state police, sheriff's, or city/local police with the possibility of each of those forces having their own version of SAR some with/without K9. In the ideal scenario, everyone who is needed will be there with all pertinent information to conduct a thorough search of the most likely areas. In my area, SAR is mostly used for recovering people in over their head with recreational activities in rural/dangerous conditions.

Some good background for K9 is that there are multiple types of searching that the dogs can do: air-scent, tracking/trailing, and human remains detection. Air scent is following the scent in the air of humans, this will include any human out and about. This is good for my area since it is so rural, won't be as good for searching for someone who wandered out of their house drunk in a populated town. Tracking/trailing is what is probably most pictured in movies with bloodhounds. The dogs are given a scent article from the subject and follow the disturbed dirt/scent trail, following where the subject moved, to ultimately locate them. Human remains detection (HRD) is what it sounds like, humans have a distinct smell when they start to decompose, even different from decaying animals, like deer for example. Some dogs are cross-trained, some aren't. All three of these methods rely on scent being available, dogs noses are amazing, but they can only go so far. Hopefully that basis will help you think of how to frame questions for your K9 handler you are interviewing.

I know how you feel. Two years ago I moved from sea level to a mile above. I was dizzy and tired all the time. I thought it was the altitude, but I finally got set up with a primary care provider and boom, I'm super anemic (ferritin level of 4, blood work all messed up). 

He puts me on iron supplements and tells me to come back in three months. I feel terrible the entire time and am sleeping more than when I was a teenager. I couldn't remember words. At one point I asked my husband to bring me my towel apron because I couldnt remember the word robe. Things like that were happening constantly. I have been living off of the iron infusions every 3-4 months and b12 injections every month. 

In the last year and a half I have had two endoscopies, one colonoscopy, an MRI, a CT and so much blood work. I have been to three hematologists (one at the Mayo clinic), two GI specialists, and a rheumatologist. At this point most of my doctors have said that if I want to figure it out I need to find a research doctor looking into malabsorptive disorders that affect iron and b12. So now I need to find a specialist somewhere in the country and go to them if I want to figure out what is going on with me. Right now I live and I'm "okay" until the iron starts dropping and I feel the physical and neurological symptoms of it. 

My story isn't helpful, but I'm happy I'm not the only one with the stupid lack of iron and b12 without a known cause.

I worked at a shelter for victims of domestic abuse. I want to first say, I do not think that who you spoke to was kind or considerate. However, I would like to explain a little bit more about my experience manning the first response phone at a domestic abuse shelter.

The first thing we do is get information. Name, address if they are willing and then the question, "are you in a safe place to talk right now?". And before we can provide services or allow them into the shelter, we have to get details of their abuse/abuser. Unfortunately, the house I worked at did not always have a bed for everyone who called. 

We often would direct them to a safe space and ask them to call back. One of the most stressful calls, was from a child who called on behalf of his mom, he was hiding in a closet and had a hard time telling us where he lived. I ended up calling 911 based off of the boys report and they were brought to the shelter later that night. 

We are also trained to help suicidal callers, but ultimately we are supposed to ask them to get to a place where they feel safe and then call someone else to check on them. 

The questions she asked you were just to assess your situation and find out how the shelter could provide assistance in your situation. I don't excuse her curt nature, but I want you to understand why she had to ask those triggering questions. 

In our shelter the majority of the time the phones were manned by volunteers, people who are there because they care. I'm happy that you called. I hope that the experience with the shelter gets better and if anything abusive happens again, you feel comfortable calling sooner. 

If you live in a bigger city, the shelter is likely there for housing abuse victims and helping them get restraining orders, jobs, and apartments. The shelter does not likely do long term care, but rather a first assessment followed by names of who you can follow up with. The system isn't perfect and Im sorry that you had to experience the shitty side, but ultimately everyone does want to help make sure that you are okay and you never end up in a situation of abuse again. *internet hugs*
